CNC JOB SHOP QUOTING · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What does that part actually cost you to make?

A job-costing calculator for CNC machine shops. Put in your stock and how many parts come out of it, your cycle time, your setup and programming hours, your tooling life and any outside process, and get the real cost per part, the break-even price, the margin at what you were about to quote, and the same part costed at every lot size from a one-off to 500. The quantity curve is the whole point: a 5-off is not a 500-off with a smaller number on it.

Everything runs in this browser. Your shop rates, your material prices and your customer's part dimensions are never uploaded — see the privacy note in the footer.

How this is worked out

Material is a step, not a rate

A bar that yields 53 parts costs the same whether you cut 31 or 53 out of it. So the material figure here is the number of whole bars or sheets you have to buy, not the weight of the finished parts — and when the stock you are buying holds more parts than you are starting, the tool says so, because that material is already paid for.

Scrap is an integer

To ship 10 good parts at a 3% fallout you start 11, which is a 10% hit and not a 3% one. The shortcut of multiplying by one plus the scrap rate understates it at every quantity: at 10% fallout, 100 good parts need 112 starts. This page uses the yield form and rounds up to a whole part.

Setup, programming and first article are per lot

They cost the same at 5 pieces as at 500, which is the entire reason a short run is expensive per part. Programming is spread over the parts you expect off the program rather than only this lot, because a reorder owes no new CAM time. Whether to bill that block as its own line or fold it into the part price is a real decision with consequences either way — setup fee or in the part price works through what each choice does to your quote and your reorders.

An outside-process minimum behaves like a second setup

Anodising at $2.10 a part with a $75 lot minimum is $15.00 a part on a 5-piece run. The minimum, not the rate, is what prices a short run, and the tool charges it on the parts you send out rather than the parts you ship — a plater does not refund the ones you scrap afterwards.

Already quoting out of a spreadsheet?

Most job shops are, and it is a reasonable thing to do — a sheet holds the history, the customers and the estimates you built over years, and this page holds none of that. What a sheet makes easy is the four costing errors above, all of which move the cost the same way on short runs. This calculator vs. quoting in a spreadsheet sets out what each tool is for, and shows the same $38 part price earning 57.4% margin at 50 pieces and losing 19.3% at 10.

What it does not do

It does not know what your market pays, what your material is worth today, what a reasonable cycle time is for your machine, or what your competitor quoted. Every number above comes from your own invoices, payroll, tooling records and machine monitor. It is arithmetic on your figures, not a benchmark.

Questions shops ask

How do you calculate a CNC machining price per part?

Add the material actually consumed, the machine and operator time for the cycle plus handling, the perishable tooling worn making the part, and any outside process. Then add the work that happens once per lot no matter how many parts you make — setup, program proveout, first-article inspection — and divide that by the lot size. Add your overhead as a percentage of that direct cost, and the result is your cost per part. Price above it by the margin you need. This calculator does that arithmetic on your own numbers; what the customer will pay is a separate question it cannot answer.

Why is a 5-piece order so much more per part than 500?

Because setup, programming and the first-article report cost the same at either quantity. Four hours of dialling in a fixture and proving out a program is four hours whether you then cut 5 parts or 500. Spread over 5 pieces that can exceed the machining itself; over 500 it rounds to cents. Quoting both off one price list is the most common way a job shop loses money on the short run, which is why the break table on this page costs the same part at every standard lot size.

How much material do I actually pay for on a machining job?

Whole stock units, not the weight of the parts. A 12 ft bar that yields 53 pieces costs the same whether you cut 31 out of it or 53, so material cost per part is a step function rather than a rate: the 32nd part costs nothing in material and the 54th costs a whole new bar. This calculator computes yield from the bar length less your chuck grip and end loss, divided by the part length plus the parting cut — or from a plain rectangular nest for plate, tried both ways round — and then charges you for the bars or sheets you actually have to buy.

How should I handle scrap allowance when quoting?

As an integer, because that is what it is. To ship 10 good parts at a 3% fallout you do not start 10.3 parts, you start 11 — which is a 10% hit on material, machine time and outside-process cost, not 3%. The common shortcut of multiplying the quantity by one plus the scrap rate also understates it at any quantity: at a 10% fallout, 100 good parts need 112 starts, not 110. This calculator uses the yield form and rounds up, and tells you the effective rate when the rounding makes it materially worse than what you entered.

Should I bill setup as a separate line or bury it in the part price?

Either works, and the calculator shows the consequence of each. A separate setup line keeps the per-part price comparable between quantities and matters most on repeats: a second order off the same program owes no new programming and often a shorter setup, so a shop that buried those in the per-part price has to explain why the reorder is cheaper. Enter what you actually bill as a setup fee and the break-even figure adjusts to only the flat work the per-part price still has to carry.

Does anything I type here get uploaded?

No. Every calculation runs in this browser, and nothing you enter is sent anywhere — there are no accounts, no cookies, and no analytics vendor. Your shop rates and a customer's part dimensions never leave the device. If you use the save button, your numbers are written to this browser's own local storage on this device only, and the forget button deletes them. Anonymous feature counts are stored the same local way and can be switched off.

setup-fee-or-in-the-part-price.html.text:
CNC JOB SHOP QUOTING

Should a CNC shop charge setup separately or build it into the part price?

Setup, programming and first-article inspection cost the same whether the order is 5 pieces or 500. Where you put that money in the quote does not change what it costs you — but it changes what the customer compares, what a reorder is worth, and whether you can still tell a short run from a long one six months later.

Should I charge setup separately or build it into the part price?

Both are legitimate and shops do both. A separate setup line keeps the per-part price comparable across quantities and makes a reorder honestly cheaper, which is why it suits shops with repeat business. Burying setup in the part price gives the customer one number to compare against other quotes, which is why it suits one-off and prototype work where the customer is shopping on part price alone. What matters is knowing which you did: a shop that buried setup and then quotes a reorder off the same per-part price is giving away the setup it no longer has to do.

What actually counts as setup on a CNC job?

The work that happens once per lot no matter how many parts come out of it. Fixturing and workholding, tool setting and offsets, dialling in the first good part, and the first-article inspection with its paperwork. Programming is in the same family but behaves differently, because a reorder off the same program owes no new CAM time at all while it usually does owe a fresh setup. That is why they are worth tracking as separate numbers even if you bill them as one line.

How do I work out what the setup fee should be?

Add the hours: setup, program proveout, and first article. Multiply by your burdened labour rate, and add your machine rate for the hours the machine is tied up and not cutting, because an occupied machine is unavailable for other work. That total is what the lot has to recover before a single part is profitable. If you bill it as its own line, the per-part price only has to clear the variable cost. If you do not, divide it by the lot size and add it to every part.

Why does the same part cost so much more per piece on a short run?

Because that flat block is divided by a smaller number. Four hours of setup, programming and first article at a burdened rate is the same dollar figure at 5 pieces as at 500, so it can exceed the machining itself on a short run and round to cents on a long one. This is not a pricing preference, it is arithmetic, and it is the single largest reason a job shop loses money on small orders it quoted off a production price list.

Is a minimum order quantity better than a setup fee?

They solve the same problem differently. A minimum order quantity refuses the lot sizes where the flat work dominates, which protects your margin but turns away prototype work that often becomes production work later. A setup fee accepts the small lot and prices it honestly, which keeps the door open at the cost of a quote with two numbers in it. Many shops run both: a setup fee as standard, and a minimum below which the setup fee alone would be more than the customer will entertain.

Should a repeat order pay setup again?

Usually some of it. A reorder off an existing program owes no programming and often no first article if the customer accepts the original report, but it almost always owes a fresh setup, because the fixture came off the table and the tools went back in the crib. Shops that keep dedicated fixtures on the shelf for repeat parts are buying down exactly this cost, which is a reason to track setup and programming separately even when you bill them together.

The same flat block, spread over four lot sizes

Suppose setup, programming and first article come to 6.7 hours. At a burdened labour rate of $35.28 an hour plus a $22 machine rate on the 2.5 setup hours, that block is about $291 — the same dollar figure at every quantity below.

Lot sizeFlat blockPer partWhat the customer sees
5$291$58.20a part price that looks absurd, or a setup line that explains it
25$291$11.64still the largest single line in the quote
100$291$2.91noticeable, not decisive
500$291$0.58rounds away against the machining

Those are the example figures from the calculator, not a benchmark. Your own hours and rates will put the crossover somewhere else, which is the number worth knowing.

Work it out on your own numbers

The calculator takes your setup, programming and first-article hours, your burdened wage and machine rate, and shows what the flat block costs per part at every standard lot size — alongside what happens to your break-even price when you move that money into a separate setup line.

vs-quoting-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
This calculator vs. quoting in a spreadsheet

Almost every small job shop quotes out of a spreadsheet, and that is a reasonable thing to do. This page is not an argument that you should stop. It is an account of which job each tool is better at, and of four specific costing errors a quoting sheet makes easy — because all four move the cost the same way on short runs, against the shop.

Open the calculator

One price list, two very different jobs

Here is the whole argument in one row of arithmetic. Take the calculator's own default job — a turned part off 12 ft bar, 4.2 min cycle, 2.5 h setup, 3 h programming, 1.25 h first article, 3% scrap — and quote it at a flat $38 a part, the kind of number a shop carries in its head or in the top row of a sheet:

Lot sizeParts startedCost / partMargin at $38
12$374.80−886.3%
56$81.94−115.6%
1011$45.34−19.3%
2526$23.3738.5%
5052$16.1757.4%
100104$12.7166.6%
250258$10.5972.1%
500516$9.9073.9%

The same part price is a healthy 57.4% margin at 50 pieces and a 19.3% loss at 10. Between one piece and five hundred the cost per part moves by a factor of nearly thirty-eight. None of that is a discount; it is the same costs divided differently. A price carried across lot sizes is wrong in both directions at once — it loses money on the short run and it is uncompetitive on the long one.

What each one is for

Your quoting spreadsheetThis calculator
Holds the quote history, the customer, the part number, and which quotes you won and at what priceHolds nothing. It costs one job and forgets it.
Carries years of your own estimates for similar partsHas no history and cannot estimate a cycle time for you
Feeds a purchase order, a traveller, or a job packetFeeds your clipboard
Formulas you wrote, which you can audit and changeOne fixed cost model, shown line by line so you can check it
Break rows usually built by adjusting one computed rowEvery break row is the whole cost re-derived at that quantity
Scrap, stock yield and lot minimums are in there if you remembered to put them inAll three are applied every time, whatever the quantity

Read that as a division of labour rather than a scoreboard. The spreadsheet is your record; this is the arithmetic check you run before a number goes into it.

The four errors a quoting sheet makes easy

1. Break rows scaled instead of re-derived

The common pattern is to compute one per-part price and adjust it for the other quantities — a few per cent off for the bigger lot, or a setup-over-quantity term copied sideways. That is an approximation of re-deriving the cost, and it drifts, because the cost curve has corners in it. In the table above the per-lot share of cost falls from $189.42 a part at one piece to $0.59 a part at five hundred, and it does not fall smoothly: the other three errors below are exactly the corners a copied formula cannot see.

2. Scrap treated as a percentage

Scrap is an integer. To ship 10 good parts at 3% fallout you do not start 10.3 — you start 11, which is a 10% hit on material and machine time, not 3%. At 50 pieces the same 3% means starting 52, an effective 4%. The rate you typed is never the rate you pay on a short run, and the gap is invisible in a percentage.

3. Material divided as a rate instead of stepped

Material is bought in whole stock units. At the default figures a 12 ft bar yields 53 parts, so a 50-piece order buys one bar and a 100-piece order buys two — the 54th part costs a whole new bar, and the 53rd costs nothing extra. A sheet that divides a bar price by an ideal parts-per-bar figure misses both edges: it over-charges the part that rides on stock you already own, and under-charges the one that forces another bar.

4. Outside-process lot minimums ignored

Anodising, heat treat, plating and passivation are quoted per part and billed against a lot minimum, so on a short run the minimum is what you actually pay. At $2.10 a part with a $75 lot minimum, a 5-piece run costs $15.00 a part and a 100-piece run costs $2.10 — the minimum, not the rate, prices the short run. A sheet that multiplies the per-part rate by the quantity is short by $64.50 on that 5-piece job, and it is short by most on exactly the runs where the margin is thinnest.

The practical suggestion

Keep the spreadsheet. Cost the next few jobs in both and compare at the smallest quantity on the enquiry — that is where all four errors are largest and where a difference will show up first. If the numbers agree, your sheet is sound and you have learned something worth knowing. If they do not, the line-by-line breakdown in the calculator will show you which of the four it is.

Cost a job both ways

On whether that setup cost should be its own line on the quote or buried in the part price, see should a CNC shop charge setup separately or build it into the part price?

Common questions

Should I stop using my quoting spreadsheet?

No, and this page is not an argument that you should. A spreadsheet is the better tool for everything this calculator deliberately does not do: keeping a quote history, holding customer and part numbers, tracking which quotes were won and at what price, feeding a purchase order or a job traveller, and carrying the estimates you built up over years of running this shop. What a spreadsheet is not good at is being re-derived correctly at a new quantity under time pressure. The honest division is that the spreadsheet is your record and this is your arithmetic check: cost the part here, then put the figures into the sheet that holds the job.

What does the calculator do that a spreadsheet formula usually does not?

Four things, all of them structural rather than clever. It re-derives the whole cost at each quantity in the break table instead of scaling one computed row. It rounds scrap up to whole parts, because you cannot start a third of a part. It buys material in whole stock units, so cost per part is a step function rather than a rate. And it applies outside-process lot minimums, which behave like a second setup on a short run. Each of the four moves the cost in the same direction on short runs, against the shop, which is why leaving them out is expensive rather than merely imprecise.

Why would a spreadsheet get the price breaks wrong?

Because the usual way to build a price-break row in a sheet is to take the per-part price you already computed and adjust it — a few per cent off for the bigger lot, or a setup-divided-by-quantity term copied sideways across the columns. That is an approximation of re-deriving the cost, and it drifts, because the amortisation is not the only thing that changes with the quantity. The scrap round-up steps to whole parts, the material steps to whole bars or sheets, and an outside-process minimum stops applying somewhere along the row. A copied formula draws a smooth curve where the real cost has corners in it.

Is my data safer in the spreadsheet or in this page?

Both stay on your own machine, so neither is a disclosure risk by itself. This page and the calculator run entirely in your browser: nothing is uploaded, there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and anything the calculator saves is written to your own browser's local storage. A spreadsheet file is equally local until you email it. The practical difference is not privacy but durability — a spreadsheet is a record you keep, and this is a calculation you run and close, which is the division the first answer above describes.
